extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students/scholars of poetics and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic (and related) poetry according to Aristotle's Poetics: definitions, constituent parts, formal constraints (unity, time, metre), and practical rules for plotting, characterization, diction, song, and spectacle. Useful for dramatists or literary critics applying Aristotelian standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action (not of narrative); through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'language embellished' (rhythm, harmony, song) and present the action through enacted scenes rather than mere narration; aim to arouse pity and fear and achieve a cathartic effect. Evaluate as a whole: seriousness, completeness (a coherent whole), and appropriate magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Diction (lexis), Thought (dianoia), Spectacle (opsis), and Song (melopoiia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts together determine the quality of a tragedy; some are medium (song, diction), some manner, some objects. Knowing and assessing each part is necessary to judge a tragedy's goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (Mythos) — unity and arrangement of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action — that is, the arrangement or composition of the incidents. The chief element of a tragedy is the arrangement of the actions (the plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a coherent, unified plot with a clear beginning, middle, and end; arrange incidents causally and organically. Sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes. Contrast episodic structure with epic narrative; avoid loose or episodic assemblages. The quality of the plot is the greatest determinant of the play's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and magnitude of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The action represented must be complete and whole, and of a certain magnitude (size), appropriate to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot includes all necessary parts to form a whole (not fragmentary) and that its scale is neither trivial nor excessively vast for the tragic form. Tragedy commonly aims to confine itself to roughly one revolution of the sun (unity of time) or slightly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication (δέσις) and Denouement (λύσις)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the Complication (δέσις) and Dénoûement (λύσις) of the Plot, especially the Denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a well-motivated complication and a satisfying resolution; the dénouement should follow from prior actions and probability/necessity, not feel abrupt or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition: its various kinds (mentioned as a component of plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognitions (discoveries) appropriately within the plot to produce impact and to transform the action; consider different forms of recognition (personal, factual, etc.) and how they interact with reversal and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid passages that are 'out of place' or forced solutions (the 'Deus ex Machina').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve the plot by improbable, external, or arbitrary contrivances that are not grounded in the established action; ensure causes and effects arise from the plot's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) — qualities and believability
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; character and thought are the natural causes of actions. The rule of necessity or probability applies to Character as to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose dispositions, decisions, and speech naturally produce the plot's actions; characters should be consistent with what is probable or necessary within the world of the play. For tragedy, characters often represent men 'better than in actual life' (idealised) but must remain believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — intellectual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (διάνοια) is the intellectual element revealed in dramatic speeches, required wherever a statement is proved or a general truth enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speeches and argumentative moments to present reasoning, themes, and beliefs; thought should clarify motivations and themes and can produce dramatic turning points (e.g., proofs, arguments, revelations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis) and Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction means the metrical arrangement of words; Poetic Diction covers the words and modes of speech admissible in poetry (including metaphor). Diction often falls within the art of delivery rather than of poetry itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose language that balances elevation and perspicuity: the words should be appropriately poetic (metaphor, elevated phrasing) but still clear. Attend to parts of speech, grammatical details, and the suitability of poetic modes; delivery affects diction's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (Melopoiia) / Music
rubrics_metrics.description: Song is the musical element (melody) entering into language; some parts are rendered through the aid of song and melody, and song has a manifest power in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate song and musical elements organically into parts of the play where they enhance imitation; distinguish metrical arrangement (diction) from song (melody). Use melody and rhythm to augment emotion and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) — visual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (the outward show or sight) will be a part of tragedy since the imitation involves persons acting; spectacular equipment and visual presentation are components of the tragic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appropriate stagecraft and visual elements, but recognize spectacle is more mechanical and less the poet's primary art; spectacle should support and not substitute for plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium, Objects, and Manner of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts differ in (1) the medium (rhythm, language, harmony), (2) the objects (types of men acted), and (3) the manner (narration vs presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the proper medium(s) (rhythm, language, harmony) for the intended imitation, choose suitable objects (portray men better/as/worse than life according to genre), and decide manner (act as living persons or narrate). Consistency among these choices defines the genre's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Type portrayed (better/worse/as they are)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation must be men of a higher type, a lower type, or as they are; Comedy commonly represents men worse than in life, Tragedy better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the moral pitch of characters appropriate to genre: tragedy elevates characters above ordinary life (noble actions), whereas comedy exaggerates faults. This affects tone, moral emphasis, and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and Measure appropriate to form
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry admits one metre (hexameter); Tragedy and Comedy employ combinations of metre, rhythm, and song; iambic measure fits colloquial speech and became appropriate for dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metres appropriate to the genre and the speech: iambic lines suit colloquial dialogue and dramatic speech; epic requires hexameter for its narrative form. Meter should support tone and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Truth and Plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Truth (the 'plausible air' of fiction) differs from common reality; one poetic principle is the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plausibility within the work's own logic over literal factual accuracy. Critics' objections about factual truth should be answered by demonstrating poetic truth — internal consistency, convincing causes, and verisimilitude of character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical composition rules for the Tragic Poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules include: (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae; (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before full composition, dramatising and physically imagining scenes and performing roles helps achieve vividness and sympathy; outline the plot structure first, then elaborate episodes, dialogue, and choral parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus and Choral Odes as organic parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate the chorus and its odes so they arise naturally from the plot and character action; avoid treating the chorus as an ornamental or detachable element. Choral elements should contribute to the imitation and overall unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcharging Tragedy with Epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the differences between epic and tragic forms: avoid excessive descriptive or narrative detail that belongs to epic; keep the tragic focus on enacted action, immediacy, and concentrated structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite varied forms of poetic excellence where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: To unite, if possible, varied forms of poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, combine strengths (plot, character, diction, music, spectacle) to elevate the work; seek balance among the parts rather than excellence in only one area at the expense of the rest.
